base_method_text.title: FiT: Flexible Vision Transformer for Diffusion Model
base_method_text.summary:
Nature is infinitely resolution-free. In the context of this reality,
existing diffusion models, such as Diffusion Transformers, often face
challenges when processing image resolutions outside of their trained domain.
To overcome this limitation, we present the Flexible Vision Transformer (FiT),
a transformer architecture specifically designed for generating images with
unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios. Unlike traditional methods that
perceive images as static-resolution grids, FiT conceptualizes images as
sequences of dynamically-sized tokens. This perspective enables a flexible
training strategy that effortlessly adapts to diverse aspect ratios during both
training and inference phases, thus promoting resolution generalization and
eliminating biases induced by image cropping. Enhanced by a meticulously
adjusted network structure and the integration of training-free extrapolation
techniques, FiT exhibits remarkable flexibility in resolution extrapolation
generation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the exceptional performance
of FiT across a broad range of resolutions, showcasing its effectiveness both
within and beyond its training resolution distribution. Repository available at
https://github.com/whlzy/FiT.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces Flexible Vision Transformer (FiT), a novel transformer architecture for diffusion models, enabling image generation at arbitrary resolutions and aspect ratios. Key contributions include a flexible training pipeline that avoids image cropping, a unique transformer architecture for dynamic token length modeling using 2D RoPE, and a training-free resolution extrapolation method using VisionNTK and VisionYaRN.
base_method_text.methodology: FiT builds upon the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture, incorporating 2D Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) for flexible resolution handling. It replaces the traditional Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with Swish-Gated Linear Unit (SwiGLU) and uses Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) to manage padding tokens. The method also employs training-free resolution extrapolation techniques like VisionNTK and VisionYaRN, adapted from length extrapolation methods in large language models.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The model was trained on the ImageNet dataset with a maximum token length of 256. Evaluation was performed across various resolutions and aspect ratios, both within and beyond the training distribution. Performance was measured using Frechet Inception Distance (FID), sliced FID (sFID), Inception Score (IS), Precision, and Recall. The FiT-XL/2 model was trained for 1.8 million steps.
base_method_text.limitations: The FiT-XL/2 model was only trained for 1.8M steps, and its performance at the training resolution of 256x256 is slightly inferior to DiT-XL/2, which was trained for more steps. The generative capabilities of FiT-XL/2 with higher resolution training (larger token length limitation) have not been thoroughly explored. The research only explores training-free resolution extrapolation techniques.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future work includes exploring the generative capabilities of FiT when trained with higher resolutions and larger token length limitations. It also includes delving into resolution extrapolation methods that require additional training. The authors suggest further research could focus on generating images with arbitrary resolutions and aspect ratios.

add_method_texts.title: Factorized Diffusion: Perceptual Illusions by Noise Decomposition
add_method_texts.summary:
Given a factorization of an image into a sum of linear components, we present
a zero-shot method to control each individual component through diffusion model
sampling. For example, we can decompose an image into low and high spatial
frequencies and condition these components on different text prompts. This
produces hybrid images, which change appearance depending on viewing distance.
By decomposing an image into three frequency subbands, we can generate hybrid
images with three prompts. We also use a decomposition into grayscale and color
components to produce images whose appearance changes when they are viewed in
grayscale, a phenomena that naturally occurs under dim lighting. And we explore
a decomposition by a motion blur kernel, which produces images that change
appearance under motion blurring. Our method works by denoising with a
composite noise estimate, built from the components of noise estimates
conditioned on different prompts. We also show that for certain decompositions,
our method recovers prior approaches to compositional generation and spatial
control. Finally, we show that we can extend our approach to generate hybrid
images from real images. We do this by holding one component fixed and
generating the remaining components, effectively solving an inverse problem.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces Factorized Diffusion, a zero-shot method that adapts diffusion models to control individual components of an image during generation. It enables the creation of perceptual illusions like hybrid images, color hybrids (changing appearance in grayscale), and motion hybrids (changing with motion blur) by manipulating noise estimates conditioned on different text prompts for each component. The method also extends to solving inverse problems, such as generating hybrid images from real images.
add_method_texts.methodology: The method modifies the sampling procedure of diffusion models. It decomposes an image into components and, during the reverse diffusion process, estimates noise multiple times for each component, conditioned on different text prompts. A composite noise estimate is then assembled from these components and used to perform the diffusion update step. The core technique involves manipulating the noise estimate rather than the noisy image itself.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The method was evaluated on tasks such as generating hybrid images (including triple hybrids), color hybrids, and motion hybrids. Qualitative results are presented for various prompts and decomposition parameters. Quantitative evaluations include a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) human study comparing the generated hybrid images to those produced by traditional methods, and CLIP alignment scores to measure the alignment of generated images with the text prompts.
add_method_texts.limitations: The method can produce images that are out-of-distribution for the diffusion model, leading to inconsistent quality. One component's prompt may dominate the generated image. The method relies on pixel diffusion models, as image decompositions must be done in pixel space. Success rate depends on careful prompt selection and parameter tuning.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research directions include studying the societal and ethical considerations of better controlling image synthesis, especially regarding potential applications in misinformation. Exploring methods to improve the consistency and quality of generated illusions, and addressing the limitations related to prompt dominance and the reliance on pixel diffusion models are also potential future directions.

base_experimental_code: The core code for the FiT model is located in `fit/model/fit_model.py`, `fit/model/modules.py`, `fit/model/norms.py`, and `fit/model/rope.py`. These files define the Flexible Vision Transformer architecture, its building blocks (like FiTBlock, PatchEmbedder, and FinalLayer), normalization layers, and the 2D Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) implementation.
base_experimental_info: The experimental settings, including training datasets and configurations, are primarily found within the `train_fit.py` and `sample_fit_ddp.py` files, and are loaded using `omegaconf`.  Specifically, training parameters related to the dataset (e.g., ImageNet), diffusion process, and model architecture are configurable through YAML files loaded by `omegaconf`. The code also shows the use of class-free diffusion guidance (CFG) with a `cfg_scale`.
new_method:
Here is a concise proposal that merges the core ideas of FiT (Base Method) with a factorization‐based sampling approach (inspired by Factorized Diffusion) to create a truly new method:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STEP 3 OUTCOME: PROPOSED NEW METHOD
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Name (placeholder): Factorized Flexible Transformer (FaFT)

1) Core Idea
   • Retain FiT’s dynamic token strategy for handling arbitrary resolutions and aspect ratios. 
   • Incorporate a factorization‐based sampling process, where the image generation is decomposed into multiple subcomponents (e.g., frequency bands, color channels), each of which can be conditioned or guided separately.
   • During inference, these decomposed noise estimates are fused within FiT’s transformer architecture to produce a single coherent image, but with finer control over different spatial or spectral properties.

2) High‐Level Workflow
   a) Multi‐Band or Multi‐Component Decomposition
      – Decompose either the conditioning signal or a latent representation into separate “bands,” such as high-, mid-, and low-frequency. Alternatively, separate color vs. grayscale, or any meaningful factorization strategy.  
      – Each band (or factor) is modeled within a dedicated branch of the FiT architecture at the same time, using shared parameters for the attention blocks but separated heads for each factor.  
   b) Factorized Conditioning
      – During training, introduce auxiliary tasks or objectives that guide each band differently (e.g., encouraging accurate reconstruction of low‐frequency content or color while independently modeling fine details for high‐frequency bands).  
      – This factorized approach leverages each branch’s noise estimate, conditioned on the relevant subcomponent.  
   c) Dynamic Token Fusion
      – FiT’s original mechanism for dynamically varying token sequences remains intact.  
      – Instead of aggregating a single attention output, the aggregator merges the separate factor‐specific outputs into a final token sequence. This merging can be implemented as a weighted combination or with a small gating network.  
   d) Resolution‐Adaptive Sampling
      – At inference time, FiT can produce images at arbitrary size (as before). Each factor’s noise estimate is computed separately (inspired by Factorized Diffusion’s composite noise construction) and then fused into FiT’s final token embeddings.  
      – Because each band is specialized, the method better preserves details in high resolutions or unusual aspect ratios, addressing FiT’s partial struggles with training resolution bias.

3) Benefits and Novelty
   • Enhanced Resolution Extrapolation: By explicitly modeling different frequency or color bands, FaFT mitigates FiT’s performance gaps around new or extreme resolutions.  
   • Flexible Partial Conditioning: One can guide only certain components (e.g., high‐frequency details) with a style or text prompt, while leaving lower bands unaltered. This surpasses simple cropping or single‐prompt conditioning.  
   • Improved Training Efficiency: Factorized objectives can help the model converge more stably when scaling to larger token lengths, potentially narrowing FiT’s performance gap at its “base” training resolution.  
   • Multi‐Use Inference: As in Factorized Diffusion, FaFT’s factorization allows “perceptual illusions” or selective transformations (e.g., color shifts that only appear under grayscale or motion blur). 

4) Example Use Cases
   • Generating extremely wide‐aspect images while preserving fine details.  
   • Creating multi‐resolution illusions where each frequency subband uses a separate prompt (e.g., different textures seen when viewed up close vs. far away).  
   • Adapting to unusual color metadata (e.g., IR or hyperspectral data) by dedicating color‐band factors.

By combining FiT’s token‐based flexibility with the multi‐component noise decomposition strategy, FaFT is both novel and more robust than the original FiT alone, addressing resolution and detail‐preservation challenges through factorized guidance during generation.
